question: How would you scale a service that is getting too much traffic?

scenes.sub: Bigger machine, more machines, or split the data.
scenes.say: Scaling a service. Interviewers want an order of operations, not a buzzword list. Find the bottleneck first, then pick the cheapest fix.

scenes.head: Think of a busy shop
scenes.say: Think of a shop with a long line. You can hire a faster cashier, or you can open more checkouts. A faster cashier has a limit. More checkouts keep growing, but they all share one warehouse, and that becomes the next bottleneck. That's scaling in one picture.

scenes.head: Vertical vs horizontal
rows: Bigger machine: more C P U and R A M
More machines behind a load balancer
No single point of failure, near linear growth
Hardware ceiling, and one box can die
App must be stateless, more moving parts
scenes.say: Vertical scaling means a bigger machine. Vertical is simple and needs no code changes. Horizontal scaling means more machines behind a load balancer, with no single point of failure. The limits: vertical hits a hardware ceiling, and horizontal needs your app to be stateless. In practice, start vertical, then go horizontal.

scenes.head: Stateless app servers behind a load balancer
scenes.say: The load balancer spreads requests across identical copies of the app. Add a third copy and capacity grows. One dies, and traffic simply goes to the others. This only works if the app is stateless: no user data in local memory or local files. Sessions and cache live in a shared store, and durable data lives in the database.

scenes.head: The database is the real bottleneck
scenes.say: App servers are easy to copy. The database is not. Writes go to one primary, which copies its data to read replicas. Send reads to replicas, but remember they can lag slightly. When even the primary can't keep up on writes or size, you shard: split rows across databases by a key, like user id. Sharding is powerful, but it makes joins and transactions across shards hard, so it comes last.

scenes.head: Order of attack
scenes.say: First, measure to find the bottleneck. Then take cheap wins: indexes and caching. Next, scale out the stateless app tier. Then add read replicas. Shard last, because it adds permanent complexity. Also mention queues for slow work, and a C D N for static files.

scenes.head: In the interview
rows: Any server can serve any request, so copies are interchangeable
Reads may be slightly stale, read your own writes from primary
High cardinality, even spread, like user id
Sharding or adding servers before measuring
scenes.say: Likely follow-ups. Why stateless? Any server can serve any request. Replica lag? Reads can be slightly stale, so read your own writes from the primary. How to pick a shard key? High variety and even spread, like user id. The common mistake: scaling or sharding before measuring the bottleneck.

lines: Vertical is simple but capped. Horizontal needs stateless apps behind a load balancer.
Keep state out of the app: sessions in Redis, data in the database.
Database path: indexes and cache, then read replicas, then sharding last.
scenes.say: Vertical scaling is simple but capped. Horizontal needs stateless apps behind a load balancer. Keep state out of the app: sessions in Redis, data in the database. For the database, go indexes and cache first, then read replicas, and sharding last. And always measure before you scale.
